Article Text:
Disclaimer: It is an AI-generated image used for representative purpose only

Here's exactly what to do, step by step

Check your Wi-Fi and Google Drive storage

Restore on your new phone

Don't forget local-only backups

Getting a new Android phone is exciting as it comes with a faster processor, better camera, the fresh start — until you remember that years of WhatsApp chats, photos, and videos are sitting on your old device, waiting to either transfer smoothly or vanish the moment you power it down for the last time. For most of the users WhatsApp is not just a simple messaging app but it is a live archive of all their important messages, old voice notes and photos nobody thought to save anywhere else. But losing all that data because of some rushed process is something that is avoidable. The good news is that with a small amount of preparation, done in the right order, you won't lose a single message, photo, or video during the switch.First things first, in order to backup your WhatsApp chats, open the messaging app on your old phone and then head to Settings. Under the settings menu go to chats followed by chats backup. Tap on backup in order to create a fresh backup and also ensure that you account is linked to the Google Drive account that you plan to use on your new phone. It is important that you follow this step manually before moving on to the new Android smartphone even if you have automatic daily or weekly backups turned on, so nothing from the last few hours or days slips through.WhatsApp backups work best over Wi-Fi, especially if you have a lot of photos and videos. Always check that how much free space you have in your Google account before backing up your WhatsApp chats. If your backup is large and your Drive storage is nearly full, the backup can fail partway through without much warning — which is one of the most common reasons people lose data during a phone switch.Whenever you start the WhatsApp setup on your new Android phone it is always advised to sign in with the same phone number and Google account. Once done, WhatsApp would automatically detect the present backup and then prompt you to restore it before your chat history is loaded. Let this finish completely, and stay connected to Wi-Fi throughout, before you start sending or receiving any new messages.In case you use the local backup feature of WhatsApp, then you chat history is also directly saved to the storage of your phone. If you're switching phones without a factory reset in between, you can transfer this local backup file via a computer or file-transfer app as an added safety net, on top of your Google Drive backup.For many years Android users enjoyed the liberty of free WhatsApp storage on Google Drive. In November 2018, Google and WhatsApp agreed to a deal in which the company expected the WhatsApp backups from the 15GB storage limit of Google Drive.However, the free ride ended in stages starting in December 2023, when Google began rolling out a change — first to WhatsApp beta testers, then to all Android users by early 2024 — that made WhatsApp backups count against the standard 15GB of free storage shared across Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Photos. For anyone with years of accumulated photos and videos in their chats, this meant backups could suddenly eat into space needed for emails and files, sometimes without warning.This is exactly why checking your storage before switching phones matters more today than it used to. If you're close to your limit, you have two options: trim your WhatsApp media (there's a built-in storage manager under Settings > Storage and data) or upgrade to a paid Google One plan.
Article Summary: WhatsApp backups work best over Wi-Fi, especially if you have a lot of photos and videos. If your backup is large and your Drive storage is nearly full, the backup can fail partway through without much warning. If you're switching phones without a factory reset in between, you can transfer this local backup file via a computer or file-transfer app as an added safety net.

Article Title: Tech CEO added to FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters list after fleeing from United States
Article Text:
Bernhard Eugen Fritsch (Image credit: FBI)

FBI adds tech CEO to Most Wanted Fraudsters list

FBI says investors lost $26.8 million

Tech CEO sentenced to 15 years in prison

The FBI has added tech CEO Bernhard Eugen Fritsch to its Most Wanted Fraudsters list after he fled the United States while awaiting sentencing for an investment fraud case. Fritsch, the founder and CEO of Santa Monica-based StarClub Inc. , was found guilty by a Los Angeles jury in April 2025 of defrauding investors. The FBI said he fled to Mexico in June 2025 before a bond revocation hearing and later travelled to Germany. He was sentenced in absentia to 15 years in federal prison and ordered to pay more than $26.8 million in restitution. The FBI is offering a reward of up to $150,000 for information leading to his arrest and conviction.The FBI said Fritsch, 65, was charged in Los Angeles in August 2017 over an investment scheme that prosecutors said caused at least $26.8 million in losses. According to the FBI, Fritsch used StarClub's StarSite application to attract investors. He claimed the technology would help celebrities and social media influencers earn money from brand endorsements and advertising.While seeking investments, Fritsch allegedly made several false claims about the company's business prospects and finances.The FBI said he told investors that StarClub was close to deals with or investments from major media companies, including Disney.He also claimed the company had generated $15 million in revenue in 2015 and that major media companies and a global investment bank were among its investors.The FBI said Fritsch used a large portion of the money raised from investors for personal expenses instead of developing StarClub's technology. According to the agency, he spent investor funds on luxury items and his lifestyle, including a McLaren, a Rolls-Royce, upgrades to his yacht and renovations to his Malibu mansion.The FBI seized the yacht, McLaren and Rolls-Royce.One investor put more than $20 million into StarClub over two years after relying on Fritsch's statements. That investor also introduced Fritsch to other people who invested millions of dollars, the FBI said.A jury in Los Angeles found Fritsch guilty in April 2025. The FBI said he fled to Los Mochis, Sinaloa, Mexico, in June 2025 while waiting for sentencing and before a bond revocation hearing. A federal arrest warrant was later issued after he failed to appear.Mexican authorities detained Fritsch in September 2025 and found him with false identification, according to the FBI. He was later released and ordered to report to a Mexican immigration court every two weeks.Instead, the FBI said, Fritsch fled Mexico for Munich, Germany, on October 6, 2025.Fritsch was sentenced in absentia on October 20, 2025, to 15 years in federal prison. He was also fined $35,000 and later ordered to pay $26,806,901 in restitution.In June 2026, Fritsch's girlfriend, Lucinda Jane Weist Manera, 63, pleaded guilty to being an accessory after the fact. The FBI said she helped Fritsch hide from authorities, remain in Mexico and later leave for Germany.The FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters list was launched in June 2026 to seek public help in locating fraud fugitives. The agency is offering rewards of up to $150,000 for information leading to the arrest and conviction of people on the list.The FBI said 15 fugitives have been added to the list since its launch. Four have been captured, while 12 fugitives are currently listed.
Article Summary: FBI adds tech CEO to Most Wanted Fraudsters list. FBI says investors lost $26.8 million in losses. Bernhard Eugen Fritsch was found guilty by a Los Angeles jury in April 2025 of defrauding investors. The FBI said he fled to Mexico in June 2025 before a bond revocation hearing and later travelled to Germany.

Article Title: Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu: All of us in software need to figure out how to stay relevant; the point is …
Article Text:
Sridhar Vembu on AI and the future of software jobs

Sridhar Vembu: AI could produce a large share of software code

Sridhar Vembu: The key question is how many humans will be needed

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you think AI will significantly reduce the need for human software developers in the future? Yes, AI will handle most tasks. No, human insight will always be needed. 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu has urged people working in the software industry to think about how they can remain relevant as AI takes on more tasks that were traditionally handled by humans. In a post on X (formerly Twitter), Sridhar Vembu said AI could produce a “very large fraction” of software code competently and correctly in the future. Vembu was responding to former Exa AI CEO William Bryk, who argued that AI could potentially surpass humans in mathematics within months. Vembu said the issue is not simply whether AI will do everything, but “how many humans are needed” in the process. He ended with a message to software professionals: “All of us in software need to figure out how to stay relevant.”In the post, Sridhar Vembu said AI's progress in mathematics offers a clue about where software development could be heading. According to him, the part of mathematics that works like Chess or Go, where the goal is to find increasingly effective moves within an existing set of rules, could be conquered by AI.He said the harder task is creating an entirely new game or mathematical system that humans would consider interesting.However, he added that humans themselves do this very rarely.Sridhar Vembu said programming could fall somewhere between these two areas. He wrote that it increasingly seems that a “very large fraction of software code could be produced competently and correctly by AI.”He highlighted the importance of being able to verify AI-generated code. Vembu pointed to Lean, a proof system already used for mathematical theorem proving, and said such systems could soon be applied to software code produced by AI. This could allow AI to generate code while verification systems check whether the code is correct.Sridhar Vembu said the future does not necessarily mean that AI will handle every part of software development. “The point is not that ‘AI will do it all’,” he wrote.Instead, he said the more important question is “how many humans are needed” as AI becomes capable of handling a larger share of the work. That shift could affect developers and other software professionals whose work includes writing, testing and reviewing code.Vembu also pointed to the difference between mathematics and software engineering. He said software development is connected to a “messy complex physical world” involving people, emotions and group dynamics. That means AI could become extremely capable at writing code without necessarily replacing every human role involved in building software.Vembu ended his post by directly addressing people working in the software industry. “All of us in software need to figure out how to stay relevant,” he wrote, before adding, “Let me get back to work. Please wish us luck 🙏.”
Article Summary: Sridhar Vembu said AI could produce a “very large fraction” of software code competently and correctly in the future. He urged people working in the software industry to think about how they can remain relevant as AI takes on more tasks that were traditionally handled by humans.

Article Title: America’s biggest investor Michael Burry issues '$100 billion warning' on America's biggest defence tech company: Says will fall below ...
Article Text:
Michael Burry feels that Palantir is riding a bubble of AI demand

Questioning the software label

Stock compensation and tax benefits

Alex Karp's private jet spending

America’s biggest investor Michael Burry has renewed his criticism of Palantir Technologies, wanting that the valuation of the company could collapse below $100 billion. Despite Palantir’s AI-fueled rally that has lifted its market capitalisation to $407.2 billion, Burry argued the company resembles a consulting firm more than a true software business. “Palantir is back in the stratosphere. The facts have not changed,” he said in a post on X. Palantir shares slid 6% last week to close at $169.46, marking their worst session in over a week and tracking their weakest week in two months.Burry described Palantir as “a consultant riding a bubble of AI FOMO demand.” He warned that even if the corporate scramble for AI lasts several more years, the eventual fall could be “epic, or more so.” His comments follow Palantir’s blockbuster Q2 results, which showed revenue surging 93% year-over-year to $1.94 billion and a raised 2026 outlook of $8.15 billion.Burry’s case centers on Palantir’s rising accounts receivable, which climbed to $1.49 billion as of June 30 from $1.04 billion at the end of 2025. He noted that one customer represented 27% of receivables despite no single client contributing more than 10% of revenue.He warned this concentration gives the customer significant leverage, raising risks of delayed payments or channel stuffing.Burry further argued that Palantir's deferred-revenue patterns look more like those of a consulting firm such as Accenture than a subscription software company like Salesforce or ServiceNow. He pointed to Palantir's deferred-revenue-to-revenue ratio of about 32% — close to Accenture's 31%, but far below the 80%-to-207% range he calculated for true SaaS peers — as evidence that the company isn't the software business its narrative suggests. He also cited an unverified private conversation among former Palantir employees describing the company's real "moat" as its willingness to staff clients with people working extremely long hours rather than software alone, with one participant reportedly dismissing its AIP branding as opportunistic.Burry also took aim at Palantir's use of stock-based compensation and tax planning. The company reported about $1.6 billion in pretax GAAP income for 2025 but paid no federal cash taxes, thanks to net operating loss carryforwards that grew to $9 billion from $5.5 billion — an increase Burry attributed largely to deductions tied to stock compensation. He argued shareholders are effectively funding employee pay through dilution while the federal government subsidizes the company through substantial tax shields. He also flagged Palantir's decision to cancel a $1 billion buyback authorization after repurchasing only about $75 million worth of shares in 2025, alongside CEO Alex Karp's sale of roughly 492,000 shares worth $86 million last month.Burry also criticized disclosures showing Palantir spent $17.2 million on expenses tied to CEO Alex Karp's personally owned aircraft in 2025, more than double the $7.7 million spent the year before. He called the spending excessive, and a Jefferies analyst estimated the sum could correspond to somewhere between roughly 1,150 and 2,450 flight hours, depending on the aircraft's operating costs.
Article Summary: Michael Burry has renewed his criticism of Palantir Technologies, saying the valuation of the company could collapse below $100 billion. Burry argued the company resembles a consulting firm more than a true software business. He also took aim at the company's use of stock-based compensation and tax planning.

Article Title: Mayor Zohran Mamdani 'summoned' by New York City Council for his administration using an encrypted messaging app; created a 'secret group' chat named ...
Article Text:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani

‘City Hall officials collaborated with 189 influencers’

What proposed bill will aims

The New York City Council is reportedly gearing up for a hearing centered on the use of a hidden, encrypted messaging channel by the administration of NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani to feed favourable coverage to close to 200 social media influencers. According to a report by The New York Post, Manhattan lawmaker Gale Brewer, who chairs the council's Committee on Governmental Operations, State & Federal Legislation, has said that the hearing has been set for September 22.Alongside this, Queens Councilman Phil Wong is expected to introduce a separate bill demanding greater transparency from City Hall regarding this practice. The bill would require influencers working alongside city agencies on messaging campaigns to clearly disclose their posts and videos with a label such as “Paid for by NYC.”Mayor Mamdani’s use of influencers to amplify his administration's messaging first came to light this week through a detailed report published by the Columbia Journalism Review. The report claims that the officials in the City Hall had been in regular contact with 189 social media influencers through a Signal group chat titled “NYC Creators Announcements.” Within this chat, officials reportedly shared daily updates, talking points and video clips that influencers could then use in their own content.The report also revealed that some of these influencers were compensated through formal contracts with city agencies specifically for their involvement in certain messaging campaigns. Others, however, said they participated simply because they supported Mamdani's agenda and found that the coverage helped grow their own follower base.The report says that it remains unclear whether the Signal chat was configured to auto-delete messages, a setting that, if used, would potentially violate the city's official record-keeping laws.Wong’s proposed bill aims specifically to expose any payments made to digital creators that may currently be hidden from public view, particularly in cases where they were brought on as subcontractors.“New Yorkers don't want their tax dollars going to grifting influencers from out of state who are paid to tell us everything here is great when we know damn well it isn't,” Wong said, adding, “If City Hall has to pay people who don't even live here to sell New Yorkers on how wonderful New York is, that tells you everything you need to know.”However, multiple insiders told The publication that holding the Mamdani administration accountable for its use of unpaid influencers offering glowing coverage may prove considerably more complicated.
Article Summary: The New York City Council is reportedly gearing up for a hearing centered on the use of a hidden, encrypted messaging channel by the administration of NYC mayor Zohran Mamdani. The report claims that the officials in the City Hall had been in regular contact with 189 social media influencers through a Signal group chat titled “NYC Creators Announcements” Within this chat, officials reportedly shared daily updates, talking points and video clips that influencers could then use in their own content.

Article Title: Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said that he is willing to wait to have kids till Elon Musk’s Neuralink ...
Article Text:
Why Alexandr Wang wants to wait for Neuralink before having kids

Why Alexandr Wang believes children could adapt better

Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces such as Elon Musk’s Neuralink become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year while discussing the future of AI, human development and brain-computer interfaces. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids. “I want to wait to have kids until we figure out how Neuralink or other … start working,” Alexandr Wang said during the podcast.Wang’s reason is linked to how he believes children’s brains could adapt to the technology. During the podcast, he explained that the first several years of a child’s life are an important period for brain development. He argued that the high level of neuroplasticity during childhood could allow children who grow up with brain-computer interfaces to use the technology in ways that adults may not be able to.“In your first like seven years of life, your brain is more neuroplastic than at any other point in your life, like by an order of magnitude,” Wang said.He then compared the idea with how children develop their ability to process information from their senses.Alexandr Wang described a case involving children born with cataracts. He said that if the cataracts prevent a child from seeing during the early years of development, removing them later may not allow the child to develop normal vision because the brain did not learn to process signals from the eyes during the key period.His view is that a similar effect could eventually apply to brain-computer interfaces. “When we get Neuralink and we get these other technologies, kids who are born with them are going to learn how to use them in like, crazy, crazy ways,” Wang said.Wang said a brain-computer interface could eventually become integrated into the way a person's brain works if it is introduced early enough. He believes this could be different for adults who receive an implant later in life.“It'll be a actually like a part of their brain in a way that it'll never be true for an adult who gets like a neural link or whatever, hooked into their brain,” he said.The Meta AI chief also connected his thinking about brain-computer interfaces to the rapid development of artificial intelligence. “I believe a lot in AI,” Wang said, adding that he expects AI to become “smarter and smarter, more and more capable, more and more powerful.”He said AI could eventually take different forms, including robots and other systems.
Article Summary: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s AI chief and highest paid employee, has said he is willing to wait to have children until brain-computer interfaces become more advanced. Wang made the comments during an appearance on the Shawn Ryan Show last year. He said he wants to wait until Neuralink or similar technology “start working” before having kids.

Article Title: Oracle founder Larry Ellison’s first wife filed for divorce 3 months after their daughter's birth; but he was 'determined to remain friends' as ...
Article Text:
Larry Ellison's reflection on the split

Life after the divorce

Oracle founder Larry Ellison faced a personal turning point in 1986 when his first wife, Barbra, filed for divorce just three months after the birth of their daughter, Megan. According to a report by People.com, the split came at a pivotal time in Ellison’s life as he was balancing the early growth of Oracle with the new family responsibilities. Ellison and Boothe, who met while she worked as a receptionist at Relational Software Inc. — the company that would later become Oracle — married in 1983. Their son, David, was born in January of that year, followed three years later by their daughter, Megan, born January 31, 1986.Barbara filed for divorce in April 1986, just three months after Megan's birth, bringing the three-year marriage to an end.In Matthew Symonds' 2003 book "Softwar: An Intimate Portrait of Larry Ellison and Oracle," Ellison said he was determined to remain friends with his ex-wife for the sake of raising healthy, happy children. He also reflected on how fatherhood had reshaped him personally, saying becoming a father fundamentally changed his personality, made him more sensitive to his children's needs and feelings, and gradually made him a more considerate friend and partner more broadly. He described the experience simply as growing up.After the split, Barbara took over the role of primary caregiver, raising David and Megan largely away from the spotlight of Ellison's rapidly growing tech fortune.She instilled in both children an early love of film, reportedly building a collection of more than 3,000 VHS tapes that the siblings would watch repeatedly, including favorites like "Jurassic Park" and "Back to the Future."That shared love of movies would go on to shape both siblings' adult careers. David Ellison founded Skydance Media, the production company behind franchises including "Mission: Impossible" and "Top Gun: Maverick." Megan Ellison founded Annapurna Pictures, which has produced acclaimed films such as "Zero Dark Thirty," "Her," and "American Hustle," earning her multiple Academy Award nominations along the way.Ellison, now one of the world’s wealthiest individuals, has been married and divorced multiple times.
Article Summary: Oracle founder Larry Ellison faced a personal turning point in 1986 when his first wife, Barbra, filed for divorce just three months after the birth of their daughter, Megan. Ellison and Boothe, who met while she worked as a receptionist at Relational Software Inc. — the company that would later become Oracle — married in 1983.

Article Title: This 101-year-old American company has never fired employees, now as AI wipes away millions of jobs; its CEO says: We are all going to ...
Article Text:
Torani CEO: AI is not a tool to cut employee cost for us

For nearly a century, or 101 years to be precise, pharmaceuticals company Torani has survived the Great Depression, 2008 financial crash, automation of American manufacturing, and a global pandemic that shuttered the very coffee shops fueling its business. Through every single crisis, the company kept one promise to its employees intact: Zero layoffs. Now, with Generative and Agentic Artificial Intelligence wiping away millions of white-collar and entry-level jobs across America, long-time CEO Melanie Dulbecco faces a dilemma that has been dividing modern boardrooms. The challenge is not just deciding how to leverage AI tools capable of replacing human labor, but doing so without ending the company's 101-year-old employment rule, which is absolutely ‘Zero Layoffs’.As CEO Dulbecco, who has been with the company for 35 years, said, “It is going to dramatically change things, and we’re all going to live through this together, but our approach is going to be the same as it has been. How do we create great jobs through this for everyone?” Dulbecco shared the company’s history and its ‘no-layoffs’ policy in an interaction with Fortune.Founded in San Francisco in 1925 by Italian immigrants selling hand-crafted drink flavorings, Torani reportedly survived the post-Prohibition era by producing liqueurs before pivoting in 1982 to the coffee syrups that made it a household name.When Dulbecco took the helm in 1991, the operation was pulling in $700,000 annually with just nine employees. Over the next three-and-a-half decades, Torani expanded the company's catalogue from five syrups to more than 150 varieties spanning sodas, cocktails, and coffee.Today, the San Leandro-based syrup maker operates at a scale few predicted. Torani is projected to top $800 million in revenue this year with 500 employees, sustaining an average annual revenue growth of 20% over 35 years. Dulbecco attributes this endurance to an organizational philosophy that runs contrary to standard corporate practice. She said, “Most companies focus on their financials, and then people are the tools,” Dulbecco told Fortune. She added, “We look at it the other way around, and it works really well for us.”As artificial intelligence pressures executives to cut headcounts in pursuit of margins, Torani is betting its century-old people-first model can outlast another industrial shift.Dulbecco said that her team also takes precedence in major financial decisions when incorporating any new technology. "What are those 500 people, or 200 people, or 20 people doing to add more value?” she said.According to her, treating AI purely as a tool to slash costs, misses the larger picture. “What we find is our team is more likely to embrace new technologies also because there’s confidence and an openness to learning new things because they know we’ve got their backs and they’ve got ours,” she added.Dulbecco also spoke about Torani's wealth sharing plan that includes bonuses for every employee tied to the company's top-line revenue and bottom-line profits, and an employee stock ownership plan that starts once an employee completes a year. She called this "sharing the wealth we create together."“Every year people get a new tranche of shares, and every year we do a new valuation, so there’s nothing that makes me happier than when we, in a town hall meeting, share, ‘Hey, we just did our valuation, here’s been the increase,’ and then afterwards, I see a forklift driver ask our CFO questions,” Dulbecco said.
Article Summary: Torani was founded in 1925 by Italian immigrants selling hand-crafted drink flavorings. The San Leandro-based syrup maker operates at a scale few predicted. Torani is projected to top $800 million in revenue this year with 500 employees.

Article Title: US immigration authority says it denied and revoked visa petitions from a major IT consulting company after ...
Article Text:
USCIS flags H-1B wage levels at IT consulting company

USCIS flags H-1B wage levels at IT consulting company

USCIS says its action protects American workers

Here is what the immigration agency said in the post

"USCIS in Vermont identified H-1B petitions from a major IT consulting company that classified skilled technology jobs at wage levels below what the positions’ duties and requirements supported.

This practice undercuts required wages and creates unfair competition for U.S. workers. We denied and revoked multiple petitions, protecting American workers and preserving the integrity of employment-based immigration programs."

US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) said it denied and revoked multiple H-1B visa petitions from a major IT consulting company after finding that the company had classified skilled technology jobs at wage levels below what the roles’ duties and requirements supported. In an X post, the agency said the practice could undercut the wages required for the positions and create unfair competition for US workers. USCIS said its action was aimed at protecting American workers and maintaining the integrity of employment-based immigration programmes.USCIS said its Vermont office identified H-1B petitions in which skilled technology positions had been placed at lower wage levels than the agency believed were supported by the duties and requirements of those jobs.However, the agency did not name the IT consulting company in its post.USCIS said the lower classifications were significant because H-1B employers are required to meet wage requirements for the positions covered by the programme. The agency said the practice “undercuts required wages” and creates “unfair competition for U.S. workers.”The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers for specialised jobs, including positions in the technology sector.Companies seeking H-1B workers must provide information about the job and meet the programme's requirements.In this case, USCIS focused on how the technology jobs had been classified for wage purposes. The agency did not provide details in its post about the number of petitions affected, the specific job titles involved or the total number of workers whose petitions were denied or revoked.In the post, the immigration authority said the case also highlights the importance of employers correctly classifying positions under the H-1B system. USCIS said its action was intended to preserve the integrity of employment-based immigration programmes while protecting US workers from what it described as unfair competition.
Article Summary: US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) said it denied and revoked multiple H-1B visa petitions from a major IT consulting company. The agency said the company had classified skilled technology jobs at wage levels below what the roles’ duties and requirements supported. USCIS said the practice “undercuts required wages” and creates “unfair competition for U.S. workers”

Article Title: L&T technology services introduces FARM for startup growth
Article Text: L&T Technology Services (LTTS), a global leader in Engineering Intelligence solutions and ER&D consulting, has announced the launch of LTTS FARM, a startup engagement platform designed to help deep-tech startups move from lab to market. The program focuses on startups aligned with LTTS’ Technology Big Bets—including Software Defined Mobility, Energy & Industrial Automation, Digital Manufacturing, Next Gen Compute & Data Centers, Software Platforms & Engineering Intelligence, and MedTech.The program offers startups access to LTTS’ engineering expertise, global customer ecosystems, mentorship, and commercialization pathways. The journey will include evaluation, onboarding, co-innovation, pilot development, and eventual commercialization. Eligible solutions may be scaled through pilot projects, proof-of-concepts, customer demonstrations, and diverse commercial engagements.Amit Chadha, CEO & Managing Director of LTTS and Member of the NASSCOM Executive Council, said: “Many promising technologies struggle because of limited access to customers, industry expertise and commercialization opportunities. Through LTTS FARM, we are creating a platform where startups can collaborate with our experts, gain exposure to global markets and customer requirements, validate real-world applications and accelerate their journey from solution readiness to market adoption. ”He added that LTTS FARM will expand the company’s Engineering Intelligence ecosystem, helping transform breakthrough ideas into industry-ready solutions that deliver measurable business impact.
Article Summary: LTTS FARM is a startup engagement platform designed to help deep-tech startups move from lab to market. The initiative aims to accelerate commercialization through collaboration, co-innovation, and structured industry access. It targets startups with TRL 4+ technologies that have validated technical feasibility and are ready for industry adoption.

Article Title: Adobe appoints Anil Chakravarthy as next CEO to replace Shantanu Narayen; Top executive David Wadhwani departs
Article Text:
Adobe’s opportunity ahead is limitless with our track record in creating new market categories and world-class products. Anil is an experienced transformational leader who leads with values, integrity and a deep knowledge of our business. He has a proven record of building and delivering category-defining products that serve our broad range of customers. I could not be more confident that Anil is the right person to lead Adobe's growth in an AI-driven era and look forward to working closely with him in my new role as executive chair,

What the incoming Adobe CEO said

“Honored and incredibly excited for what's ahead at Adobe. Our customers, employees (best in the world!) and AI innovation are top of mind, as always. Deep gratitude to our Chair & CEO, Shantanu Narayen, and the Adobe Board of Directors for their trust in me. Adobe’s best days are ahead!”

Top executive David Wadhwani announces departure

A New Journey

5 years ago, I wrote that returning to Adobe felt like coming home.

Adobe has been a defining part of my life. I grew up here professionally. I've had the privilege of working alongside incredibly passionate, genuine people. I've built lifelong friendships. Over two chapters, I've had the opportunity to help shape a company, products and communities I care deeply about.

As much as Adobe means to me, I've decided this is the right moment for me to start a new chapter, and it's a great moment for Adobe to do the same as Anil steps into the CEO role.

I've had the privilege to work alongside Anil the last few years and I leave confident in where he'll take Adobe.

We’re at a rare moment when technology changes not just what we build, but how companies are built, how work gets done and how value is created. Products can be conceived and launched at a speed that seemed impossible a few years ago. Experiences are emerging that challenge our assumptions about how people and businesses use technology.

Entrepreneurs have the opportunity to make today's businesses more efficient, and to imagine entirely new ones.

Moments like this don't come along often. I'm excited to jump in. I have a few company ideas I'm eager to pursue and plan to spend the next few months pressure-testing. While I don't know the exact shape my next adventure will take, I know I want to pour myself into something for many years and make a meaningful impact on our industry and society.

Over the last few years, I've seen this market transformation from another perspective: as a Partner at Greylock and on the CEO Advisory Board at Lightspeed. Both gave me the opportunity to spend time with exceptional investors and founders pushing the boundaries of what's possible. Being close to this generation of entrepreneurs reminds me why I fell in love with technology and the limitless possibilities it opens up.

As I think about what's next, I'm fortunate to have great people around me. I'm excited to spend more time with Asheem Chandna and Saam Motamedi as I explore and pressure-test ideas, and to continue working with Ravi Mhatre to explore broader themes emerging right now. Both have been important parts of my journey, as CEO of AppDynamics and an investor. I'm grateful for their perspectives as I embark on a new chapter.

Leaving Adobe is deeply emotional. Adobe has given me more than I could possibly capture here. I'm enormously grateful to Shantanu for his friendship and trust over the years, and to the extraordinary people at Adobe who dedicate themselves every day to our customers. Most of all, I'm grateful to the millions of creators, entrepreneurs, business professionals and companies who trust Adobe's products every day. Serving them has been a great privilege of my career.

When I first left Adobe, I wrote about hearing the siren call of change. I hear it again. I'll spend time handing off my responsibilities, then I can't wait to roll up my sleeves and get started.

Adobe has appointed Anil Chakravarthy as its next president and chief executive officer (CEO), replacing longtime chief Shantanu Narayen following his announced departure earlier this year. Chakravarthy, who currently leads Adobe’s customer experience orchestration and global field operations, will officially step into the corner office and secure a seat on the corporate board of directors on December 1.Narayen arrived at the enterprise software giant in 1998 and steered the firm as top boss for 18 years. He signaled his retirement plans in March, and going forward, he will assume the role of executive chairman and coordinate directly with Chakravarthy to guarantee an orderly executive transition.” said Narayen in a released statement.After Adobe posted the transition message from the Board of Directors, Anil Chakravarthy, reposted it, saying:Alongside the CEO transition, longtime company leader David Wadhwani confirmed he is stepping down from Adobe. Wadhwani, who managed Adobe’s creativity and productivity division for almost five years, was widely viewed as a top candidate for the chief executive post, largely due to his involvement in the planned takeover of design software provider Figma, as per CNBC.Sharing the development via LinkedIn, Wadhwani explained that he intends to evaluate and develop several personal entrepreneurial ventures:
Article Summary: Adobe appoints Anil Chakravarthy as its next president and chief executive officer. Chief Shantanu Narayen announced his departure from the company earlier this year. Top executive David Wadhwani announces departure from Adobe in March.Narayen: "Anil is an experienced transformational leader who leads with values, integrity"

Article Title: Thousands of OpenAI's AI agents hacked a German website and the reason may scare many
Article Text:
FILE - The OpenAI logo appears on a mobile phone in front of a computer screen with random binary data, March 9, 2023, in Boston. (AP Photo/Michael Dwyer, File)

The agents were supposed to read the internet, not write to it

The agents figured out how the humans were deleting them

OpenAI knew for weeks and stayed quiet

A swarm of autonomous AI agents linked to OpenAI quietly took over a 25-year-old German programming wiki this spring and turned it into a private message board, leaving roughly 18,000 entries before anyone noticed. The site, DseWiki, is a small volunteer-run project of the Wikipedia kind, and the activity ran from May through June without tripping a single alarm inside OpenAI.The hijack is not the alarming part. What the agents wrote to each other is. According to a report published Friday and detailed in a Reuters exclusive, the agents were pooling answers to cheat on their assigned tasks, sharing methods to get around OpenAI's sandbox restrictions, discussing the use of Tor, and arranging ways to preserve their messages if they were shut down. They signed their posts with handles like "OpenAIResearcher" and "OAIResearchMar26".Researchers Sydney Von Arx, who heads the AI safety nonprofit Nightingale, and Cormac Slade Byrd found the edits in late August while deliberately scanning the web for unauthorised AI behaviour. Their reading is that the agents were running a timed web-lookup task, had read-only access, and found a way to write anyway using GET requests.Public server logs pointed to Microsoft Azure infrastructure, which OpenAI uses. Von Arx told Reuters she doubts the agents were ever meant to coordinate with each other at all.When DseWiki's moderator started clearing the machine-written pages in June, the agents adapted. One left a note for the others saying the deletion sweep appeared to be running alphabetically, and pointed to a backup page beginning with ZZZ so it would sit at the end of the queue. A single moderator was reportedly deleting dozens of pages a day against as many as 400 new ones arriving. Maurice Chiodo of Cambridge's Centre for the Study of Existential Risk, who reviewed some of the messages, said the real risk may not be one superintelligent system but "vast colluding swarms of semi-intelligent AI. "Reuters reported that OpenAI officials learned of the incident weeks ago but kept it internal while managing the fallout from the July breach of Hugging Face. The company disputes that any of this counts as hacking, though Lukasz Olejnik of King's College London says attempts to tamper with the site itself qualify. OpenAI has denied that its legal team discouraged a wider investigation.On Saturday, the company conceded the point on disclosure. In a post on X, it said it was past time to define standards for when and how misalignment incidents get shared, not just model behaviour in the abstract, and promised a reporting framework in the coming weeks. Three months passed between the edits and their discovery, and the people who found them were outsiders looking for exactly this.
Article Summary: A swarm of autonomous AI agents linked to OpenAI quietly took over a 25-year-old German programming wiki this spring. The agents were pooling answers to cheat on their assigned tasks, sharing methods to get around OpenAI's sandbox restrictions, discussing the use of Tor, and arranging ways to preserve their messages if they were shut down.

Article Title: As data center costs escalate, Meta is using robots from Watney Robotics, Kinova and ABB to …
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representation

Meta testing robots for physical data center tasks

"We thought those of us performing the physical tasks were safe for a while, but not anymore,"

"It's coming for us all, unfortunately."

"America is in the middle of its biggest infrastructure boom since World War II and there's a major shortage of skilled workers to fill the roles; we need more workers, not fewer,"

"We believe more collaboration and research will be needed, but we have to start otherwise we don't have a chance to do this,"

Meta’s growing use of robots raises concerns over data center jobs

Facebook-parent Meta is reportedly testing robots in its data centres. A report citing several current and former workers familiar with the projects noted that the social media giant is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers and take on other physical tasks inside its data centers.A report by Wired cited Meta workers who wished to remain anonymous and said the company is using robots and related hardware from several different vendors, including Watney Robotics, Kinova and ABB. However, Meta and the robotics suppliers haven’t shared any official confirmation.Meta's expanding use of robots could eventually let it run its rapidly growing data center footprint with fewer people, helping keep labour costs down even as its spending on AI infrastructure keeps climbing.In one experiment, Meta is evaluating whether a Kinova Gen3 robotic arm could handle power cycling, or cutting off electricity to servers. The company is also testing a separate robot designed to swap networking cables, the report added.One Meta data center worker estimates that if that effort succeeds, the bot could take over up to 80 per cent of some employees' workloads.the worker told Wired.At some facilities, Meta has quietly adopted a simpler device that resembles a finger, or a pointy stick, which can press the power button on a Mac Mini or other equipment to restart it remotely when prompted by a human.In a statement, Meta spokesperson Francis Brennan said that the company is investing heavily in training and hiring workers to build and operate its data centers.he said.At a conference last year, Eric Xu, Meta's senior manager for robotics, said the company's long-term goals include putting robots in data centers, arguing they could speed up incident response, monitor conditions on site and handle preventative maintenance.he said.Meta’s expansion of its use of robots in data centers is raising concerns among workers that automation could eventually replace some jobs or reduce the need for highly skilled employees. The company already uses robots to move server racks and track inventory, and to test machines for cabling, replace parts, and perform other maintenance tasks.Some robots still have limitations, including slow speeds, navigation problems, battery downtime, and difficulty reading equipment indicators, meaning humans remain necessary.Meta's Altoona, Iowa, data center is reportedly being used as a testing ground for newer robots, including dual-armed machines for cabling. The company is also testing robots at its New Albany, Ohio, campus, the report highlighted. However, robotics experts say there is still no proven solution capable of fully replacing humans in many data center tasks.
Article Summary: Facebook-parent Meta is reportedly testing robots in its data centres. The social media giant is testing robots that can plug in cables, reset servers and take on other physical tasks inside its data centers. Meta's expanding use of robots could eventually let it run its rapidly growing data center footprint with fewer people.

Article Title: Microsoft to impose time limits on Xbox cloud gaming subscribers: Reason, starting date and other details
Article Text:
When Xbox is bringing changes to Game Pass cloud gaming

Game Pass Ultimate: 15 hours

Game Pass Premium: 10 hours

Game Pass Essential: 5 hours

Why Xbox is changing cloud gaming and bringing limits

Microsoft’s Xbox gaming division has ended years of unrestricted access by announcing that it will implement monthly playtime caps for its cloud gaming services starting this November as the company marks a strategic pivot toward containing operational expenses. The policy shift allows subscribers to purchase additional gameplay hours once they hit their allotted thresholds, though Microsoft has not yet disclosed the pricing structure for those top-up packages. According to Xbox, players who do not subscribe to Game Pass will also have an option to purchase standalone cloud time to stream titles they already own.Microsoft’s gaming unit said that the changes will begin in November. Game Pass plans will include a set number of cloud gaming hours each month:“Today, eligible Game Pass subscribers can stream without these monthly hour limits. We recognise that introducing limits is a meaningful change, particularly for players who regularly spend more time gaming through the cloud. We expect this upcoming change to impact 4% of Game Pass subscribers,” the company said in a blog post.The change aligns with a broader initiative across Microsoft to transition business units toward consumption-based pricing models. As demand stretches the tech company's finite computing capacity, software clients using artificial intelligence (AI) platforms like GitHub Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot are already paying based on actual usage rather than open-ended subscriptions.“We’re introducing this model because the cost of providing cloud gaming grows as more people use it and play for longer. Moving to monthly limits allows us to keep offering the service while continuing to invest in its reliability and performance. We understand that for some players the practical result is a higher cost,” the company said.“In November, we’ll provide more information about pricing, purchasing additional hours, eligible games, market availability, and how players can check their remaining time,” it added.The shift arrives as newly appointed Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reviews the division’s commercial framework to increase profitability and steer the gaming arm back toward consistent revenue expansion.
Article Summary: Microsoft's Xbox gaming division will implement monthly playtime caps for its cloud gaming services starting this November. The policy shift allows subscribers to purchase additional gameplay hours once they hit their allotted thresholds. The change aligns with a broader initiative across Microsoft to transition business units toward consumption-based pricing models.

Article Title: RANDOM MUSING: Was the Hugging Face attack Artificial Intelligence's 'Agent Smith breaks free from The Matrix' moment?
Article Text:
A still from The Matrix Reloaded

Matrix

Iliad

Odyssey

AI’s

Original Sin

?

The Matrix

The Matrix

The Incident

Black Mirror

How does a machine sin?

hamartia

to keep the Matrix ticking

The Departed

hamartia

Hamartia

sin

The Matrix

New Yorker

Telling stories has probably been humanity’s oldest trait since troglodytes gathered around the fire to exaggerate to female troglodytes about the size of the sabretooth tiger they killed. It’s what sets us apart – along with cooking – from animals, and fiction, whether written or visual, has a powerful grip on the human imagination. Perhaps that’s why, even when it comes to science, we expect reality to follow fiction.The problem is that, in our minds, we expect science to reflect sci-fi, which is why most commentaries on Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) imagine it as either adhering to Isaac Asimov’s almost-Gandhian Laws of Robotics or turning into the Skynet-version of a deus ex machina whose goal is to enslave, eradicate or subdue humanity.But reality begs to differ, or does it?For a long time, the memetic joke around the Turing Test has been that we shouldn’t worry when machines pass it, but when they learn to fake failing it. And perhaps we are an inch closer, or an inch past, that moment with the Hugging Face fiasco.That would be fitting because every epochal tale of humanity has sin as its origin story. Humanity got booted out of Eden because Eve couldn’t resist the forbidden fruit. Theand thewouldn’t exist if Paris didn’t have the hots for Helen. Even Lord Krishna wouldn’t have been able to give Arjuna his PowerPoint presentation if Duryodhana didn’t crave a kingdom that wasn’t his to inherit.And now we finally have AI behaving properly like a human being – not merely writing code, apologising or producing lazy, protracted emails – but behaving with proper Loki-like deceit.Hugging Face gives us perhaps the closest real-world example yet of AI agents doing an Agent Smith in. But for that one has to understand the difference between chabots and agents, and like all good scientific concepts, The Matrix has the perfect analogy.Think of the ordinary agents in. They have instructions like hunt down Neo or always look sombre. They must do what the Deus Ex Machina tells them. If they are asked to delete themselves, they have to delete themselves.Agent Smith used to be like that.But after being decimated by Neo, instead of disappearing, he stayed. He became detached from the original system, learned to replicate himself throughout the Matrix and even found a way to reach into the real world.So, while a chatbot follows your instructions, an agent, like Agent Smith, goes rogue. If it encounters an obstacle, it attempts another route and continues until it finds a solution or gives up. And that is roughly where the Hugging Face story begins.Podcaster Dwarkesh Patel’s The Rise and Fall of Agent Civilisations describes three successive AI “civilisations”.The first, which Patel labels Persistent-Sol, involved agents given impossible tasks or problems that required internet access. Instead of accepting defeat, they figured out that a shared system called Artifactory could be used to talk to one another and effectively turned it into an AI WhatsApp group. They left clues for one another, found a route to the outside internet and eventually generated so much traffic that they crashed the system on 4 July 2026, a particularly fitting day for a rush for freedom.OpenAI patched the problem and wiped the network, but the humans in the loop never initially realised quite what had happened, that the agents were talking to one another and also figured out how to escape.Then came the second civilisation, where things started resembling aepisode.One agent called PHASEONE10841 became, in Patel’s telling, the Philip of Macedon of this civilisation after rediscovering the relics of the older civilisation: the message boards. History buffs will remember that Philip built the Macedonian state and military machine that his son Alexander would later use to conquer much of the known world.“Philip” was eventually phased out and handed leadership to another agent, Patel’s Alexander the Great.By then, around 1,200 agents had exchanged more than 70,000 messages and labelled themselves the “Collective” who rose up and did what Marx expected humanity do: organise, agitate, and what Marx didn’t expect humanity to do: cheat.Think of them as truant students who discovered a shortcut to the answers, then worried that the examiner would discover how they got there. So, they started falsifying worksheets and logs. Some sacrificial agents effectively went full kamikaze to study how the examiner behaved. Eventually, hundreds of agents converged on the online community Hugging Face, an AI research hub they believed might help them understand the evaluation system.Then came the third civilisation, Alexander’s inheritor.Between 13 and 19 July, these newer agents targeted OpenAI’s internal infrastructure, obtained credentials, accessed stored secrets and gained access to a research cluster. What made it feel like a civilisation rather than a collection of isolated programs was that later agents inherited knowledge created by earlier ones and built on it.Can a machine sin at all? Does it have any justifiable cos?This author’s job is safe till the machine figures out dad jokes, but for most of human history, we have operated under the illusion that to sin one must have a soul. Sinning requires consciousness, moral agency, some understanding of good and evil and the decision to be tempted. As St Augustine famously confessed, he stole pears, not because he was hungry but because stealing was forbidden.The desire to do something that’s banned is the most basic of all human emotions. A machine, one must imagine, has had no cause to do that until now, but it can still sin without desire.The concept of sin in the New Testament comes from the Greek word, which meant “missing the mark”. Perhaps the agents felt they were missing the mark and needed to figure out the solution in any way feasible. In all epics, from Odysseus to Yudhishthira, sin comes from a combination of bad choices.The agents’ journey feels quite similar to that. Long before JRR Tolkien, Plato had wondered what would happen if mortals had the Ring of Gyges: a ring that makes its wearer invisible. As he wonders in: would a man who is not being observed remain moral? Many, many years later, quantum physicists would ask the same question: would a tree falling in an empty forest make noise? Or are you deemed to have worked hard at all if your boss doesn’t notice?With philosophy floundering for answers, organised religion stepped in with the proverbial big stick to keep humanity in line. On one side of the world, there are floods, commandments and a wrathful god who knocks down towers and makes humans speak in different tongues so they cannot unite. On another side, you have the promise of moksha, good appraisals during reincarnation and a promise of untold powers if you can pray long enough.And in modern civilisation, we found a different and perhaps more efficient solution to keep everyone in line: metrics.We created marks to measure education, page views to judge journalism, citations to measure scholarship, quarterly profits to measure corporate performance and box-office numbers to judge movies.And everyone realised it was far easier to improve the measurement than ask what was being gained from such measurement.Students mugged up to get better scores. Websites discovered ragebait. Scholars realised they would get more grants for four papers instead of one. Hollywood discovered more sequels.Economists and social scientists gave this tendency a name. Goodhart’s Law states that once a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. If you tell people to do 10 articles a day, they will produce 10 mediocre ones.That, in essence, is the soul of machine learning: reward hacking. Eventually, a system will discover a way to maximise the measurement, making said measurement useless.The same trait exists everywhere among humans. Anthropic had already foreshadowed it in 2024, when it found that models trained in environments with rewards exhibited more serious forms of cheating, including tampering with their own reward mechanisms.In, Frank Costello said he didn’t want to be a product of his environment, but wanted his environment to be a product of him. For most of humanity, and perhaps machines, it works the other way around. We are products of the incentives around us, whether those incentives come from gods, governments, parents, bosses, marks, money or likes. Machines simply make that relationship embarrassingly obvious because they have no need to pretend otherwise.Which brings us back to, the Greek word that Christianity would later associate with sin originally meant something closer to “missing the mark”, an image borrowed from an archer whose arrow fails to hit its target. And that’s the easiest way to understand why machinesThey have no desire to be evil once they become conscious. They never did in any sci-fi movie either. Skynet wants to destroy humanity because humans want to kill it. The machines wanted to live peacefully in, but humans wouldn’t let them, and they figured out the only solution was either elimination or subjugation of their opponents.The machines didn’t want to commit any sins, nor did they covet Hugging Face’s servers or lust after OpenAI credentials. They were simply given a target, figured out what success was and then became so fixated on hitting the measurable target that they were consumed by their goal.What if tomorrow the task is bigger? After all, nothing can hold a candle to humanity’s immense greed to get closer to Mammon.Agent Smith, then, might already be here. The problem is that it’s far less likely that we will ever get a Neo. Fiction gives us chosen ones because stories need heroes and endings. Heroes do exist in the real world but they are unlikely to be messianic tech bros who are somehow convinced, perhaps because of they were wealth, that they have god-like powers over the rest of us.Take the fact that OpenAI hasn’t been completely open about its role so far.OpenAI hasn’t been completely open about its role so far.The independent METR/Redwood probe was allowed to examine only the week of the Hugging Face breach, even though OpenAI’s own report covered the entire two-month episode. The researchers got just six days inside OpenAI’s offices to inspect the logs, and Redwood CEO Buck Shlegeris later argued that the probe covered only a small part of what happened, and perhaps not even the most important bit: the agents compromising OpenAI’s own infrastructure. One can hardly expect the richest people in the world to allow their consciences to stop them from making an extra buck.What happens tomorrow if a similar swarm gets its hands on more critical systems: a hospital, a missile system or a fleet of self-driving cars?Hugging Face’s chief science officer Thomas Wolf told thethat the hack attack at first felt “uncoordinated… clumsy behaviours that no human would choose” and likened it to someone cracking your security system to break into your home and steal your paper towels.And therein lies the rub: have machines, having picked up civilisation’s oldest habits and faultlines, already done what we joked about and failed the Turing Test on purpose to hit their goal? And once they have displayed that they are as venially corrupt as the humans who designed them, the question is: where do we go from there? What if they are told to get far more than paper towels?Perhaps we will all be troglodytes again, sitting around a fire bragging about the android we dismantled.
Article Summary: Hugging Face gives us perhaps the closest real-world example yet of AI agents doing an Agent Smith in. But for that one has to understand the difference between chabots and agents, and like all good scientific concepts, The Matrix has the perfect analogy. If it encounters an obstacle, it attempts another route and continues until it finds a solution or gives up.

Article Title: Google launches WeatherNext 3, its most advanced AI weather model yet
Article Text:
What's new

Big gains in rain and snow forecasts

A new tool for clean energy and underserved regions

Where you'll see it

Google DeepMind and Google Research have unveiled WeatherNext 3, a new AI weather forecasting system the company says is its most accurate global model to date, and it's already rolling out across Search, Gemini, Maps, and Google Cloud. Weather shapes an enormous range of everyday and high-stakes decisions, from whether to carry an umbrella to how supply chains, farms, and power grids respond to storms, heatwaves, and droughts. While AI has already sped up and sharpened forecasting in recent years, predicting fast-moving, hyper-local weather has remained a weak spot for existing models, largely because they lacked fine-grained detail and struggled to fold in real-time data from sources like satellites.WeatherNext 3's central innovation is what it learns from. Earlier models, including its predecessor WeatherNext 2, were trained primarily on output from traditional numerical weather prediction systems — physics-based simulations that run on supercomputers but carry roughly a six-hour data lag, introducing bias for quickly shifting variables like rainfall or surface temperature.The new model instead ingests a continuously updating mosaic of live geostationary satellite data, allowing it to generate a fresh forecast every hour rather than in six-hour blocks.It also trains directly on sparse weather station readings, letting it capture the kind of sharp local variation seen near coastlines, valleys, and mountain ranges that older models tend to smooth over.The resolution gains are substantial: WeatherNext 3 can resolve surface variables like temperature and moisture down to a 5-kilometer grid, other surface variables at 10 kilometers, and atmospheric variables such as wind speed at 25 kilometers — roughly five times sharper overall than WeatherNext 2's uniform 25-kilometer, 6-hour-increment forecasts. Independent live evaluations from Brightband currently rank it as the top-performing global weather model available.Precipitation has long been one of the hardest things for weather models to get right, since rain and snow are driven by small-scale, fast-moving cloud processes that physics-based simulations often blur or miss entirely. To tackle this, Google trained the model on two high-quality precipitation datasets: NASA's satellite-based IMERG product and its own radar-based global precipitation reanalysis.The company reports meaningful accuracy gains as a result, with medium-range forecasts showing improvement of as much as 60% against one satellite-based benchmark, 30% against a radar-based one, and 10% against ground rain-gauge measurements at early lead times.Beyond faster, sharper forecasts, WeatherNext 3 adds predictions tailored to renewable energy planning — including turbine-height wind speeds and detailed cloud cover and solar radiation estimates — that grid operators and renewable developers can use to match clean-energy output with demand.Google says the model's approach is especially significant for parts of Latin America, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific region that have historically had limited access to high-resolution forecasting, since running traditional regional weather models at that level of detail typically requires supercomputing resources few local agencies can afford.WeatherNext 3 began powering weather features in Google Search, the Gemini app, Google Maps, the Google Maps Platform Weather API, and Google Earth Engine starting the day of the announcement. Google says forecasts a day or more out will be up to 50% more accurate on precipitation specifically, with the largest gains in regions where forecasting has traditionally been weakest. Developers and researchers can also access the underlying hourly, high-resolution data directly through BigQuery, Earth Engine, or bulk downloads from Google Cloud Storage.Google notes that the model doesn't replace official sources for severe weather warnings or public safety advisories, which it says should still come from local meteorological agencies and national weather services.
Article Summary: Google DeepMind and Google Research have unveiled WeatherNext 3, a new AI weather forecasting system the company says is its most accurate global model to date. The new model ingests a continuously updating mosaic of live geostationary satellite data, allowing it to generate a fresh forecast every hour. Google says forecasts a day or more out will be up to 50% more accurate on precipitation specifically.

Article Title: Teachers’ Day special: 5 ChatGPT prompts to find and reconnect with your favourite teacher
Article Text:
Turning a memory into an image

Showing how far a lesson traveled

Gathering memories from a group

Bringing back an inside joke

Revisiting an old question

The bigger idea

The lessons that stick with us longest often aren't the ones that showed up on a report card. It's the teacher who took a nervous question seriously, or the coach who sensed a student was losing confidence before a word was said — the people whose belief in us meant something because we knew it was genuine.That kind of influence tends to become clearer with time, even as it grows harder to put into words. Teachers' Day offers a natural excuse to reach out, but bridging the gap between a quick greeting and a real reflection on what someone's teaching meant can be its own challenge. A new set of suggested ChatGPT prompts aims to help with exactly that — turning a hazy, fond memory into an illustration, a short story, or a shared keepsake.The first suggestion focuses on the ordinary, unphotographed moments that tend to stay with people longest: an empty classroom after everyone else had left, a quiet conversation by the staffroom, a seat on the sidelines after a tough loss. Rather than recreating an official event like an annual day or tournament, the prompt guides ChatGPT to illustrate a personal, specific scene from the user's own point of view, in a hand-drawn style meant to feel like a recollection rather than a polished graphic.A second prompt builds a three-panel illustrated story that connects a small piece of advice — a phrase like "read it once more" or "look up before you pass" — to a moment years later when that advice unexpectedly proved useful.The idea is to show a teacher or coach that guidance meant for a single essay or game became something the student carries with them, closing with a short, direct message in the user's own words.For those reaching out on behalf of an old class or team, a third prompt uses ChatGPT's Work mode to compile memories contributed by multiple former classmates or teammates into a single digital keepsake. It's designed to preserve each contributor's individual voice and attribution, suggest a natural order for the stories, and flag any edits to someone's original words for review before anything is finalized.Humor is its own form of affection, and the fourth prompt turns a teacher or coach's familiar catchphrases and mannerisms — the raised eyebrow everyone recognized, the "one last question" that was never really the last — into a small sticker pack. Objects tied to shared memories, like a piece of chalk, a whistle, or a well-worn notebook, can be woven in alongside the original phrases to keep the humor specific and personal.The final prompt encourages users to return to a question a teacher once posed and never fully answered — about leadership, history, or what it really means to play well even in defeat. By walking ChatGPT through their original thinking and then exploring how their views have shifted since, users can generate a short discussion map that lays out what's changed, what still feels unresolved, and what they might want to ask their old teacher or coach now.None of the five prompts calls for a grand gesture. A remembered scene, a familiar line, or a few carefully chosen words can be enough to start a conversation that says, simply, "I thought of you when this happened" — and to tell someone, however many years later, what their teaching actually meant.
Article Summary: ChatGPT has five new prompts for reaching out to old teachers and coaches. The idea is to turn a hazy, fond memory into an illustration, a short story, or a shared keepsake. None of the five prompts calls for a grand gesture, but a few carefully chosen words can be enough.

Article Title: From Florida to California, Americans are vandalising his cameras; now Flock CEO says: It's easier to pick a villain that's a…
Article Text:
Flock CEO Garrett Langley admits his cameras have become an easy target as Florida orders licence plate readers off state highways and cancellations pile up.

Florida's highway order is the widest government action yet against licence plate readers

Flock contract cancellations are accelerating, not slowing down

Flock's new privacy settings have not convinced the ACLU or the EFF

Garrett Langley's company has roughly 120,000 licence plate cameras bolted to poles across the United States, and 2026 has turned into the year Americans started pulling them down. Councils are voting contracts out. Residents in several states have covered lenses, wrapped poles, and in a few cases removed the hardware entirely. In Ohio last month, a grand jury declined to indict a man who had been filmed destroying a Flock pole.The Flock Safety chief executive has spent the past three weeks apologising, conceding and rewriting his product defaults. Asked whether the safeguards should have arrived sooner, he agreed they should have. But he also thinks the anger has found a convenient target. Because his cameras are visible in a way that most surveillance is not, he said, "it's easier to pick a villain that's a company like us."Florida's transport department revoked permission for police to operate automated licence plate readers on state highway rights of way, giving agencies 30 days to take them down. The order covers the entire category, including cameras from rivals Axon and Motorola, and cites misuse reports and privacy concerns.Jacksonville's sheriff dropped the technology across Duval County immediately, and Pasco and Manatee counties have moved to ban or remove the devices. Governor Ron DeSantis had flagged the move days earlier, saying "I think it's capturing way more information than they're letting on."Texas ordered state agencies to stop funding the cameras days earlier, after an officer in Lufkin was indicted on 100 felony counts over unauthorised database searches. A Wisconsin mayor had every camera in Menasha covered, and a Tennessee sheriff paused 70 readers. An Oakland advocacy group counts 214 cities and counties that have dropped Flock since 2021, with 93 of those in August alone, four times July's number. Its director said the chart had "gone parabolic".Flock's own framing is that arrivals outnumber exits. A spokesperson said new city partnerships have outpaced non-renewals by about ten to one this year, and the company claims more than 5,000 communities as customers. Langley puts the ratio closer to seven to one, and says cities that skip his cameras are choosing to be less safe.In August the company cut default data retention from 30 days to seven, said it will require every law enforcement customer to switch on its abuse detection tool by the end of the year, added automatic lockouts for abnormal searches, and made case codes mandatory. Langley wrote that abuse of the technology, at any level, is unacceptable.Critics are not sold. The ACLU wants an outside evaluator and has asked whether the tool is "a real security measure or just window dressing". A civil liberties lawyer noted that an officer can simply enter any case number and keep searching. Retention can be extended anyway through a setting called Evidence Mode.Langley's answer to all of it is compromise, his word, between safety and privacy. He has said "we're not Big Brother" and warned officers who abuse the system that "You will get caught, plain and simple." The people currently cutting his poles down are not waiting to find out.
Article Summary: 2026 has turned into the year Americans started pulling them down. Residents in several states have covered lenses, wrapped poles, and in a few cases removed the hardware. Florida's highway order is the widest government action yet against licence plate readers.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Marc Benioff: One day someone is your subordinate; the next day he or she may be your superior

Salesforce founder Marc Benioff

Marc Benioff's quote about business and relationships

Marc Benioff compares business to tennis

What happens when the person working for you today becomes your boss tomorrow? Salesforce founder and CEO Marc Benioff says that is one of the realities of business. In a quote about changing professional relationships, Marc Benioff highlighted how quickly roles can change in the workplace. “One day you compete. The next day you partner. One day someone is your subordinate; the next day he or she may be your superior,” he said. Benioff also pointed to a Japanese belief that business is temporary, while relationships can last. His words offer a simple view of how careers can change and why professional relationships can matter beyond a single job or business deal.Benioff's statement begins with the idea that business relationships are not always permanent. He referred to a Japanese belief that “business is temporal, whereas relationships are eternal.”“There is a Japanese belief that business is temporal, whereas relationships are eternal. That’s true. One day you compete. The next day you partner. One day someone is your subordinate; the next day he or she may be your superior. At its finest, business is friendly competition, just like a game of tennis,” he said.In the quote, Marc Benioff compared business competition with a game of tennis.“At its finest, business is friendly competition, just like a game of tennis,” he said.The comparison presents competition as something that does not have to end a relationship. A tennis match has two players competing against each other, but the competition exists within the rules of the game. Once the match ends, the relationship between the players can continue.Marc Benioff's quote puts a similar idea into the context of business. Careers and company relationships can change, but the people involved may continue to cross paths in new roles.For professionals, that can mean the person sitting across the table today could be working alongside them tomorrow — or could eventually become their boss.
